messages.subject: question on the ectotherm model in NicheMapR
parts:
Dear Professor Kearney,

As you suggested, I have posted our previous communications and my latest questions to this google group. Thank you again for helping me with this! Looking forward to your response.

Best,

Bingbing

 

My latest question:

Yes, I’m using the micro_era5 function. The non-default parameters include loc, dstart, dfinish and spatial (code included below). Most of those snakes were basking and did not forage that I have temperature data on. And only a few had foraged.

Here are my code for running the microclimate model and the ectotherm model respectively (I have also sent the full R script and data to you by email):

micro<-try(micro_era5(

  #Type in parameters that are not default

  spatial=spatial,

  loc=c(lon,lat),

  dstart=dstart,

  dfinish=dfinish))

ecto<-ectotherm(Ww_g=median(na.omit(dat_snake$Mass)),             T_F_min=min(na.omit(dat_snake$Tbody_measured[which(dat_snake$Foraging=="Yes")])),

T_F_max=max(na.omit(dat_snake$Tbody_measured[which(dat_snake$Foraging=="Yes")])),

T_B_min=min(na.omit(dat_snake$Tbody_measured)), #assume T_B_min=T_F_min

T_RB_min=min(na.omit(dat_snake$Tbody_measured)),

T_pref=max(na.omit(dat_snake$Tbody_measured)), #find the peak of the density plot of field body temperatures

diurn=1,

nocturn=1,

crepus=1,

climb=1,

shape=1,

shape_b=15)

 

 

Our Previous Communications: 

Dear Bingbing Liu,

Are you using the micro_era5 function? I’d start with how you are modelling the microclimate. What non-default parameters did you use for the microclimate model? Also, what do you know about what those snakes were doing that you have temperature data on? The model is good at giving you the extreme bounds on what’s possible but of course they can achieve a lot of variation within that by microhabitat selection. If you send me your whole script I can take a look. If you feel comfortable posting this on the NicheMapR google group it would be good so that others can learn from what we discuss.

All the best,
Mike


Dear Professor Kearney,

Hope this e-mail finds you well.

My name is Bingbing Liu. I am an undergraduate student at Sun Yat-sen University. I’m writing to you with regards to consulting you some questions about the ectotherm model in NicheMapR.

I have been working on a project investigating climate change impact on the activity time of a diurnal aboreal snake  using NicheMapR. However, our model validation showed that the ectotherm model overestimated the snake’s body temperature early in the morning and late in the afternoon. I will collect more field body temperature data this summer to repeat the validation. But I’m really curious about your opinion about potential directions for tunning the ectotherm model. I have included non-default parameters I used for the snake below along with a figure showing the model validation. Please see the attached file model validation figure.

Thanks for your time! Looking forward to your response. 

Best regards,

Bingbing Liu

  

Result 1

The figure below shows the actual body temperature data and the predicted body temperature data using the ectotherm model of the snake, China.

(1) The time period is from September 14, 2018 to September 18, 2018;

(2) The black hollow circle "○" represents the actual body temperature data of the snake;

(3) The solid black line represents the predicted body temperature of the snake using the ectotherm model.

 

Result 2

The figure below shows the actual body temperature of the snake in Shedao, China, and the ambient temperature data recorded by the lbutton placed on the Shedao, China.

(1) The time period is from September 14, 2018 to September 18, 2018;

(2) The Solid black dots represents the actual body temperature data of the snake;

(3) The solid lines in different colors represent the ambient temperature data recorded by lbuttons placed at different locations on the Shedao, China.

(lbuttons : lbutton1, lbutton2, lbutton3, lbutton4, lbutton5, lbutton7, lbutton8, lbutton9, lbutton10)

 

Result3

The figure below shows the predicted body temperature, activity level, shade selected and depth of the snake during a year by the ectotherm model.

messages.subject: Re: question on the ectotherm model in NicheMapR
parts:
Dear Bingbing Liu,

Thanks for the question. There are a couple of things to note. First, for the cylinder shape, which you are using, I found a problem with the code for computing surface areas a couple of months which has now been fixed. The other thing is that the model had the behaviourally thermoregulating animal orienting itself perpendicular to the sun's rays to get warm if it was in the basking state. That isn't always going to be the case (esp. for some types of organisms that are more sessile or leaves which may or may not orient). The only way to stop that was to set 'LIVE=0' but that turned off all behaviour and metabolism. So I've just made some changes (pushed to github) such that when you set 'LIVE=2', it does all the behavioural thermoregulation and metabolism but doesn't orient to, or away from, the sun as part of thermoregulation. Your snakes, being cryptic sit-and-wait predators, probably choose their position mostly to maximise the chance of catching a bird and don't want to move around posturally and break their cover. So it would be might be more appropriate to set 'LIVE=2' in which case it will be in a posture that is in between perpendicular and parallel to the sun and isn't tilting toward the sun to be maximally absorbing solar radiation.

So if you run this code instead:
ecto<-ectotherm(Ww_g=Ww_g,
                T_F_min=T_F_min,
                T_F_max=T_F_max,
                T_B_min=T_B_min, #assume T_B_min=T_F_min
                T_RB_min=T_RB_min,
                T_pref=T_pref, #find the peak of the density plot of field body temperatures

postur=0,
                live=2,
                shape_b=15)

You could also play around with the microclimate model predictions, changing the slope, aspect, roughness height, and perhaps most importantly , change the height the microclimate simulation is using (input 'Usrhyt') because the default 1 cm height might be a bit too low for a big viper. You could also increase the default percent conduction (pct_cond = 10) to something more snakey. The microclimate simulation by default is for vegetation-covered ground (cap = 1, bulk density for loamy sand if I remember correctly). The thermal conductivity calculated by the microclimate model is used as the thermal conductivity the animal experiences for conductive heat flux. You could simulate the microclimate model with cap = 0 and change the BulkDensity (and BD vector) to be a little bit lower than the Density (and DD) vectors to simulate rock. Or you can use the code I've pasted below to simulate them on a more conductive surface (but which is at the same temperature as the predicted soil surface - this is not necessarily realistic because rock would not necessarily get as hot during the day as vegetation-covered surfaces where there's insulation from the veg preventing heat flowing into and out of the soil profile).

tcond <- micro$tcond # get the conductivity matrix out
tcond[, 3] <- 2.5 # change the conductivity of the 3rd column = soil surface to a value more like rock
ecto<-ectotherm(Ww_g=Ww_g,
                T_F_min=T_F_min,
                T_F_max=T_F_max,
                T_B_min=T_B_min, #assume T_B_min=T_F_min
                T_RB_min=T_RB_min,
                T_pref=T_pref, #find the peak of the density plot of field body temperatures

postur=0,
                live=2,
                shape_b=15,
                pct_cond = 40,
                tcond = tcond) # explicitly pass this modified conductivity vector in

Re the ibutton comparison, it seems like your times are out of alignment. If I add a couple of hours to the observed times I get a better alignment (so perhaps you haven't adjusted the GMT timezone correctly from the microclimate model output).



Finally, it looks like cloud came in on the day you presented Tb and ibutton data but the ERA5 microclimate prediction doesn't have this happen. That would also be an issue with the match between observations and predictions, but with the snakes you have them thermoregulating in the simulation making it look like they were in the field. It may, from the ibuttons, that they didn't need to in reality but they did in the simulation.

All the best,
Mike
